analysis.one_liner: Requires employers moving jobs to low-wage countries to give workers 180 days' notice and severance, health, and retraining benefits.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a vote: after sitting in the House Education and Labor Committee for a year and a half, it was sent to a subcommittee in November 1994 and died when that Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: When a company of 25 or more workers closes a plant or lays off a large group because it is moving the work to a country with much lower wages or weaker labor rules, the bill would have required the company to give 180 days' advance notice and to pay each affected worker a month of severance per year of service, 18 months of continued health coverage, up to $10,000 for retraining and relocation, training stipends, and credit toward retirement. Companies that fail to comply would be barred from federal contracts for similar products, and workers, states, cities, and the Labor Department could sue to enforce it. The stated purpose was to discourage shipping jobs overseas and to soften the blow for the workers left behind.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers at factories and offices of 25 or more employees who lose their jobs because the work moves to a country paying less than half the U.S. average wage or with much weaker overtime, child labor, and safety rules. They would get long advance notice, a month of severance per year worked, 18 months of continued employer health coverage, up to $10,000 in retraining and moving costs, weekly training stipends, and enhanced retirement credit if they are near retirement age. States and cities that gave tax breaks or subsidies to keep a plant open could also claw those back in court if the plant still left.

how_it_helps.text: Employers would have to give 180 days' written notice before a plant closing or mass layoff tied to a work transfer to a low-wage country, including the reasons, any alternatives considered, and the site's profitability, so workers and communities get time to prepare [S3].

Each employee losing a job would receive severance pay equal to four weeks' wages multiplied by years of service, continuation of health coverage for 18 months, up to $10,000 for retraining, job search, and relocation, and training incentive payments [S3].
Workers within five years of retirement age would receive benefits equal to five additional years of pension accrual, cushioning older workers who are hardest to re-employ [S3].
Employers that do not provide the notice or benefits could not win federal contracts for the products or services involved in the work transfer, adding a direct financial incentive to comply [S3].

Workers could sue for lost wages plus double liquidated damages and attorney's fees, states and local governments could recover location subsidies, and the Secretary of Labor could investigate, subpoena records, and sue on workers' behalf [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Companies with 25 or more employees that move work to low-wage countries would pay severance, extended health coverage, retraining reimbursements, and retirement top-ups, plus legal exposure for double damages if they skip the requirements. Economically, these costs would fall on those employers and, potentially, on consumers through higher prices or on remaining workers if companies offset costs. Business groups argued such mandates raise the cost of restructuring and could push employers to automate or move jobs to avoid coverage, though those arguments are not in the record here.

drawbacks.text: The mandate is expensive and targeted: a month of severance per year of service plus 18 months of health coverage and up to $10,000 per worker for retraining could add substantial per-worker costs for companies restructuring toward lower-cost production, which honest supporters would have to acknowledge [S3].

The definition of a 'low wage foreign country' — any country with average wages below half the U.S. average or weaker labor standards — sweeps in most of the developing world, so the requirements would attach to a very broad range of closures and layoffs, and employers could face double damages and government suits over contested determinations [S3].

A good-faith objection: benefits triggered only when work moves abroad can give employers a reason to restructure in other ways — slow attrition, automation, or transferring work to higher-wage countries — rather than pay the mandated package, and the bill does nothing for workers displaced by those routes [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For workers facing offshoring, the benefits are substantial and concrete: notice, a month of severance per year of service, 18 months of health coverage, and funded retraining are the difference between a manageable transition and a family crisis. The costs fall narrowly on employers moving work to low-wage countries, which was the bill's point. The design is defensible — the good-faith reduction on damages, the employer's ability to prove the foreign expansion is unrelated, and the addition to existing rights rather than replacing them limit abuse — though the trigger is broad and the mandate could make employers slightly more reluctant to open U.S. plants they might later move. On balance it is a worker-protection bill whose main uncertainty is economic side effects, not fairness.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in the House Education and Labor Committee from June 1993, was sent to a subcommittee in mid-November 1994, weeks before the Congress ended, and never came to a floor vote.

narrative.text: Rep. William D. Ford of Michigan introduced the bill on June 8, 1993, and it was referred to the House Committee on Education and Labor [S1][S5].
The bill had 81 cosponsors — 80 Democrats and 1 Independent — but no Republican cosponsors [S4].

The committee never acted on the bill; on November 14, 1994, about seven weeks before the Congress ended, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Labor-Management Relations and no further action followed [S5].
No floor vote was ever held in the House and the Senate never considered it, so the bill died at the end of the 103rd Congress on January 3, 1995 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Companies that move work to low-wage countries are better off: they face no notice requirement, no severance or health-continuation mandate, and no risk of the double-damage lawsuits or federal contract bars the bill would have imposed. Workers facing plant closings keep only the pre-existing, weaker WARN Act protections.

for.name: Rep. William D. Ford
for.role: U.S. Representative, MI-15; chair of the House Education and Labor Committee
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and gave introductory remarks; it was referred to the committee he chaired, which had jurisdiction to move it.

for.name: 81 House cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill: 80 Democrats and 1 Independent.

against.name: House Committee on Education and Labor
against.what_they_did: Never reported the bill out; after 17 months it was sent to the Subcommittee on Labor-Management Relations on November 14, 1994, too late for any floor action.

sides.party_line_note: All 81 cosponsors were Democrats or an Independent; no Republicans signed on, and the bill never advanced in the Democratic-majority committee.

industries.industry: Manufacturers and other employers that move production or services offshore
industries.note: The bill would have made it materially more expensive to close a U.S. site and shift the work to a country with wages below half the U.S. average or weaker labor standards, by attaching severance, health, retraining, and retirement obligations plus double-damage liability. Its stated purpose was to discourage exactly that transfer.

Employers that failed to provide the required notice or benefits would have been barred from U.S. government contracts for the products or services involved in the work transfer, a significant consequence for defense and other federal suppliers.

industries.industry: Staffing and temporary-help and employer-side consultancies
industries.note: These firms profit when companies restructure cheaply; mandated notice, severance accounts, and retraining funds would have reduced the flexibility offshore-restructuring clients pay for. This is a secondary, indirect effect.
